title: Most sea cucumbers crawl, but the ‘headless chicken monster’ swims

cover.alt: A red sea cucumber with a frilly veil at its top end drifts in deep blue water.

body: Sea cucumbers are echinoderms, relatives of starfish and sea urchins, and most of them get around by crawling along the seafloor, swimming only as a last resort to escape predators. The deep-sea *Enypniastes* treats swimming as a way of life: by **pulsing its fin-like flaps** it lifts itself off the bottom and travels long distances to find food or escape danger. To eat, it sinks back down and scoops up sediment rich in marine snow, the organic debris that drifts down from the water above.

slides.alt: A red sea cucumber drifts in dark blue water, the frilly veil at its top end opening and closing as it swims.
slides.caption: Filmed by NOAA's robot submarine Deep Discoverer in the Gulf of Mexico in 2017: the sea cucumber Enypniastes eximia swims in open water, pulsing the frilly veil at its front.
slides.credit: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Gulf of Mexico 2017 · Public domain · excerpt

left.label: Most sea cucumbers
left.text: Crawl along the seafloor. Many can swim, but most do so only as a last resort, to escape a predator.

right.label: Enypniastes
right.text: Pulses its fin-like flaps to lift off the bottom and swim long distances, to find food or get away from danger.

slides.prompt: Remotely operated vehicle pilots named it for looking like a plucked chicken. What is its more elegant nickname?
slides.detail: Its flowing movements earned it the second, prettier name.

slides.heading: Which one is not an echinoderm?
slides.explanation: Starfish, sea urchins and sea cucumbers are all echinoderms. Jellyfish belong to a different group, the cnidarians, along with corals and sea anemones.
